quote: Yeah. I don't remember requesting that, but that's okay. You can tell me about it.
stewart_read: The rep never directly answers the implicit 'how did you get my info' question raised by the customer's line. He instead moves into explaining the design-team process (00:35) and later narrates the Google Maps pull (01:02), which functions as an indirect, transparency-based legitimacy builder rather than the schema's honest_specificity protocol (protocols.how_did_you_get_my_number) which calls for naming the lead source directly ('you filled out a form online'). Given the customer let it go without further pushback, the indirect approach worked well enough here, but it left a specific, closeable gap unaddressed.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive miss — rep simply didn't register the skepticism as something requiring a direct answer and moved on out of habit.
coaching_implication: When a customer flags they don't recall opting in, name the source directly and briefly (per protocols.how_did_you_get_my_number) before pivoting to the design-team explanation — it closes the loop explicitly instead of relying on downstream transparency cues to do that work.

quote: The roof looks awesome for solar. You got tons of space up there. It looks like you're getting, yeah, full sun all day.
stewart_read: Rep offers a positive, specific observation about the roof from Maps rather than a generic script line — a small but real personalization move that reinforces legitimacy (he's actually looking) and builds rapport simultaneously.
coaching_implication: This is a repeatable good habit — narrating a specific, real observation from the property check doubles as both a verify step and a trust builder. Worth reinforcing as a model move for other reps.

stewart_read: Customer volunteers a specific score well above the 650 threshold unprompted — a sign of comfort and forthcoming engagement the rep could have leaned into ('with a score like that you'll have your pick of financing options') but instead moved straight to the next verify item.
coaching_implication: Small moments where the customer over-shares favorable info are opportunities to build warmth with a quick acknowledgment before moving on — costs two seconds, reinforces the customer's own positive self-image about the decision.

quote: I'd say it's never less than $200 a month.
stewart_read: This is the anchor moment — a concrete, above-average bill figure. The rep acknowledges it ('Dang. Yeah. That's up there for sure.') but the acknowledgment is passive; he does not flip it into an emotional alignment-against-the-utility frame or tie it forward to the design/savings conversation.
coaching_implication: This is the single biggest miss on the call. Coach the flip: something like 'that's exactly the kind of bill this program is built to bring down' ties the number directly to urgency instead of just sympathizing with it.

quote: Yeah, just to see if we can help you save some money there on your bill.
stewart_read: This is the natural spot to flip the $200/month figure into forward-pulling curiosity ('let's see what that number could look like with solar') but the line stays generic and doesn't reference the number the customer just gave.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic — rep may be intentionally holding specifics for the closer's proposal call rather than setter-tier speculation.
coaching_implication: Even without giving numbers, the rep could tie the vague 'save some money' line directly back to the $200 figure just given, making it concrete and personal rather than generic.

quote: I'm getting ready to go inside my house. You wanna call me back in about fifteen minutes?
stewart_read: The call ends on a customer-initiated callback with no specific time locked beyond 'about fifteen minutes' and no button-up elements (hour block, no-driving anchor, is-that-fair handshake) since the appointment itself was never reached — the call never got past bill collection.
coaching_implication: When a customer proposes a loose callback window, the rep should still lock a specific clock time ('so that's 3:45, does that work?') rather than accepting 'about fifteen minutes' at face value — vague windows are harder to keep and easier to miss.
